idea.idea: Why AI agents break in production: Autonomy needs strict engineering guardrails
idea.angle: Agent failures aren't prompt engineering mistakes; they happen when you grant full autonomy without deterministic verification checkpoints.
idea.audience_problem: Business owners build autonomous agents that occasionally send incorrect price quotes or hallucinated stock counts to clients.

hooks: Why your AI agents keep making expensive mistakes
Stop letting AI agents make unsupervised business decisions
Your autonomous agent needs a circuit breaker, not more training
piece.hook_reason: It addresses the specific pain point of business owners whose automated systems (like price quoting or stock tools) fail in production, directly linking the failure to lack of guardrails.

slides.title: Why your AI agents keep making expensive mistakes
slides.subtitle: Autonomy without engineering guardrails is a recipe for business-critical errors.

slides.title: The Agent Fallacy
slides.myth: AI agents just need better prompts to work in production.
slides.fact: Access to intelligence isn't the bottleneck. The real challenge is engineering industrial-grade controls that govern how agents use tools and data.

slides.title: Why Demos Break
slides.body: Demos are net practice. Production is the match. In production, agents face real regulated data, compliance requirements, and business-critical integration points that break simple, unverified logic.

slides.title: Production-Ready Checklist
slides.body: Before deploying an agent to handle client data or pricing, ensure these four controls are active:
items: Audit trail for every decision made
Circuit breakers to halt faulty execution

slides.title: The Engineering Reality
slides.quote: Intelligence is abundant, but trust, accountability, and repeatability, we must still engineer.

slides.title: How to Stabilize Agents
items: Codify business logic with domain ontologies
Shift testing to simulate runtime stress
Measure cost per governed business outcome
Always keep human escalation as a fallback

piece.caption: When your AI agent starts quoting wrong prices or hallucinating stock levels, it is not a 'bad model' problem. It is a control problem. Moving from a successful demo to a reliable production system requires shifting focus from prompt engineering to infrastructure engineering. You need circuit breakers that can catch errors and escalate them to a human before they hit your customer's screen. If you cannot audit why an agent chose a specific price or credit limit, it is not ready for your business. Start by documenting the decision policies the agent must follow, then build the monitoring to ensure it stays within those boundaries. URL: https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/10/22/1146109/designing-an-ai-serving-harness-built-to-last/

The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.
That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”
Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.
There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.
The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't.
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost.
Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.
GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.
Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements.
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.
Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.
Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.
The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/10/autonomy-and-control-are-not-opposites-they-go-together-ey-gds-at-devsparks-chennai
Autonomy and control are not opposites, they go together: EY GDS at DevSparks Chennai | YourStory Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT Ask a room of developers about agents today and you will get plenty of answers. Almost everyone has built one, and most have a demo they are proud of.
The harder question is what happens after that, when the agent has to hold up against real customers, real data, and real consequences. At DevSparks Chennai 2026 , Arvind Purushothaman, Global Cloud Consulting, Microsoft Practice and Alliances Leader at EY GDS , opened with a version of it. He asked how many people in the room had built an AI agent, and plenty of hands went up. Then he asked how many had built one that made it to production for a business-critical system. "I think that's where the numbers dramatically drop," he said. "Not because of anybody's fault, but that's how it is."
That gap is the whole problem, and it is not a model problem. Cloud, low code tools, and open model APIs have pushed the entry barrier close to zero. What has not changed is the difficulty of industrializing what you build. "Access to intelligence is not the bottleneck, but the ability to industrialize is going to be the bottleneck," said Arvind Purushothaman.
Drawing on a cricket analogy, he said that hackathon builds are like net practice, where a few lines of Python and an API key let you rehearse your reverse scoop all afternoon. The match is different. You need 12 runs off six deliveries under pressure, and the strokes only matter alongside the ability to read the situation.
For agents, that pressure arrives when the demo meets regulated data, compliance requirements, integration points, and business-critical workflows. Skip the rigor and the exposure is concrete: a bad transaction, financial loss, reputational damage, security and privacy failures. The question itself changes, Purushothaman said, from does it work in a demo to "can we trust it repeatedly under real operating conditions."
Traditional software ran on deterministic rules and stage gates that everything had to clear before production. Agents behave differently. They interpret context, reason about a goal, and decide for themselves which tools to use to reach an outcome.
The instinct is to read it as less work for engineers. Purushothaman argued the opposite. More freedom for the agent means more engineering responsibility for the people around it, because the system has to constrain, restrict, and verify what the agent does. "Autonomy and controls … they are not the opposite of each other in this world," he said.
He offered three maturity levels to locate yourself against. Task-based agents automate specific steps and return an output. Goal-oriented agents are handed an objective, such as how much credit limit a customer should get, and assemble their own data and policies to reach a recommendation. The third horizon is humans and agents as one team, with judgment reserved for critical calls.
Three foundations make production deployment possible, and they only work together. Domain context and ontologies codify business knowledge, taxonomy, and decision logic, and mature vendors now ship them by industry. Controls evaluate outcomes for quality, bias, and risk, and produce traceability. The platform makes execution repeatable and scalable. Ontologies without controls create chaos, controls without a platform are not repeatable, and a platform without domain context is generic.
The model is only one part of the system, so the engineering has to cover data context, cloud and compute, integration APIs, security and identity, responsible AI, and FinOps discipline around cost. "The outcome is only as strong as the weakest link in your chain," Purushothaman said.
Take a customer asking a bank to raise their credit limit. The agent has to establish identity, retrieve the applicable risk policy before anything else so it knows which boundary it is operating under, pull the relevant data, and interpret context. The recommendation has to stay inside policy guidelines, and if the risk is high, it should transfer to a human. Every step has to be auditable. Without that preserved history, he said, it is not a production-ready system.
Hence the agent passport. Every agent gets an identity, a named business owner and technical owner, defined permissions covering where it can operate, and escalation points. Organizations already carry deprecated software they cannot account for, and agents will multiply that problem faster. Production systems also need circuit breakers: anomaly detection, the ability to halt execution, roll back, and escalate to humans.
Asked how to measure return, Purushothaman pushed back on counting agents deployed and tokens consumed. The number that matters is cost per governed business outcome, counting cloud and agent running costs, the human effort still in the loop, and the risk profile. "You don't want to over-engineer a simple ask, and you don't want to under-engineer a complex ask. It should be right for the outcome."
Testing, he added, has to shift from fixed test cases toward simulating production like runtime conditions. Asked whether robustness holds as attackers keep evolving, he conceded that the how will change while the fundamentals will not. "We talked about the why. We talked about the what. The how will evolve."
He closed on the sharpest line of the session. "Intelligence is abundant, but trust, accountability, and repeatability, we must still engineer."
